paras: The near-lynching of Billy Reed took place at O'Neill City, Holt County, Nebraska, in late March or early April 1881, when residents nearly lynched a cowboy held for the fatal shooting of Sheriff Barney Kearns. No one was killed; the prisoner was moved to the jail at West Point, and the local paper credited the dying sheriff's plea for forgiveness with saving him. Reed was acquitted of the murder that October, and none of the reports gave the race of anyone involved.

According to a special dispatch from Omaha to the Chicago Tribune, about ten cowboys rode into O'Neill City on March 29, 1881, "went on a spree," and disturbed an auction sale being run by Sheriff Kearns. After words passed, the sheriff took their revolvers, and the party left but soon came back. One of them, named in the dispatches as Harry Dean or Harry Deans, then shot Kearns through the heart, and the deputy sheriff was wounded in both legs. Citizens gathered to capture the cowboys, but they rode off to Neligh in Antelope County, and as of March 30 no arrests had been made.

Among its Nebraska items on April 12, the Omaha Daily Bee reported that "the people of O'Neill narrowly missed lynching the murderers of Sheriff Kearns last week." The item gave no details of the crowd, its size or how the lynching was averted, and it said that a single prisoner was now held in the jail at West Point.

A tribute reprinted from the Progress in the O'Neill Frontier of April 28 explained Reed's escape differently. After his last confession to a priest, it said, Kearns faintly said "Billy Reed killed me, but let him go," and the writer had "no doubt" that these words saved Reed from being lynched.

Feeling in the town stayed high after the shooting. In a card in the same issue, a resident wrote that a notice signed "Vigilance Committee" had been posted on his building forbidding him to sell more whisky, and that threatening notices bearing his name had later been put up around town.

By April 19 the Holt County authorities were looking for two more of the cowboys, Stuart and Smith, as accessories to the murder. On October 6 the Frontier carried a one-line notice that William R. Reed had been acquitted of the murder of Sheriff Kearns. No report was found of an inquest, of charges against Harry Dean, or of any action against those who threatened the prisoner.

The killing travelled by wire, appearing in the Chicago Tribune on March 31 under a headline reading "Murdered by Cowboys" and in the Helena Weekly Herald on April 7 under "Cow Boys." The near-lynching, by contrast, drew only Nebraska notice: one sentence in the Bee's state column and a passing remark in the O'Neill paper's eulogy.

Neither paper condemned the crowd. The Bee reported the near-lynching flatly, while the Frontier made Reed's escape a lesson in the sheriff's forgiveness, praising "a grand religion" that teaches the forgiving of trespasses. The papers called the attackers "cowboys" and "lawless cow boys" and named no race for the accused, the sheriff or the crowd.

Accounts differed over who fired the fatal shot. The Omaha dispatches named Harry Dean, or Deans, as the shooter and said another man in the party wounded the deputy. The O'Neill tribute, written closer to the scene, quoted Kearns naming Billy Reed as his killer and said the sheriff had accidentally shot his own deputy, Jim Connelly. It was Reed who was later tried and acquitted, and the Bee's item spoke of "murderers" in the plural while mentioning only one prisoner.

bases: A crowd of O'Neill residents 'narrowly missed lynching' the prisoner accused of killing Sheriff Kearns, a threatened lynching with no one killed (A5, A7).

The papers say the people of O'Neill narrowly missed lynching the accused and that he was saved and later held at West Point, so no one was killed (A5, A7); the crowd's pretext was the sheriff's murder, but its size is not given.
The Omaha Bee's state item and the O'Neill Frontier's reprinted tribute independently say the accused was nearly lynched (A5, A7); neither gives detail.
